title: Job 12:13–25
context: Job continues speaking. In a hymn-like passage he describes God's wisdom and power: God tears down and builds, withholds and releases the waters, and overturns counselors, judges, kings, priests, and nations. This is Job's argument within the dispute. He insists that he knows God's sovereign power as well as his friends do, yet he sees that power acting in ways that break their tidy formula. The passage should be read with the lawsuit Job begins in chapter 13.

verses.text: “With God is wisdom and might. He has counsel and understanding.
verses.arminianNotes: "With God is wisdom and might." Arminian readers see Job affirming God's greatness, while noting that he speaks it as part of an argument with his friends, not as a quiet hymn of praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that wisdom, might, counsel, and understanding all belong to God. Job knows this as surely as his friends, but he will soon press God himself to explain his dealings.

verses.text: Behold, he breaks down, and it can’t be built again. He imprisons a man, and there can be no release.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, he breaks down, and it can’t be built again." Arminian readers hear Job describing God's power from the perspective of someone who feels torn down himself, with no visible reason given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that no one can undo what God does, whether in tearing down or imprisoning. Job describes God's sovereignty as overwhelming and, from where he stands, frightening.

verses.text: Behold, he withholds the waters, and they dry up. Again, he sends them out, and they overturn the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, he withholds the waters, and they dry up." Arminian readers see drought and flood as examples of God's control over creation, which can bring both blessing and devastation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same God who withholds the waters "sends them out, and they overturn the earth." Job stresses God's freedom in both directions. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: With him is strength and wisdom. The deceived and the deceiver are his.
verses.arminianNotes: "With him is strength and wisdom. The deceived and the deceiver are his." Arminian readers read this as Job saying that no one, not even a deceiver, stands outside God's rule, without making God the author of deceit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read it as God's sovereignty over all people, including those who deceive. The site's earlier note on Judges 9:23 discusses God and evil agents; Job's line here makes no new claim beyond that.

verses.text: He leads counselors away stripped. He makes judges fools.
verses.arminianNotes: "He leads counselors away stripped. He makes judges fools." Arminian readers see Job noting that God humbles even the wise and powerful, which undercuts the friends' confidence in their own counsel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal of status: counselors and judges, who should be wisest, are led away and made foolish. Human wisdom is no defense against God.

verses.text: He loosens the bond of kings. He binds their waist with a belt.
verses.arminianNotes: "He loosens the bond of kings." Arminian readers see God removing the power and authority of rulers, whose authority depends on him, not on themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often compare Daniel 2:21: "He removes kings and sets up kings." Even kings are bound and humbled at God's pleasure. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: He leads priests away stripped, and overthrows the mighty.
verses.arminianNotes: "He leads priests away stripped, and overthrows the mighty." Arminian readers note that even religious leaders are not exempt from God's overturning power, so religious standing gives no guarantee.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the list now includes priests and the mighty. Every class of leader stands under God's hand, which is exactly why Job's friends cannot claim special insight.

verses.text: He removes the speech of those who are trusted, and takes away the understanding of the elders.
verses.arminianNotes: "He removes the speech of those who are trusted." Arminian readers see God taking away the words of trusted advisers and the understanding of the elders, an implied rebuke to the friends who claim the wisdom of age.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the link with verse 12: the elders whom tradition honors can lose their understanding at God's word. Wisdom is God's to give and to withdraw.

verses.text: He pours contempt on princes, and loosens the belt of the strong.
verses.arminianNotes: "He pours contempt on princes." Arminian readers note that Psalm 107:40 uses the same words, "He pours contempt on princes," showing that Job draws on language Israel also used in praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job's line "loosens the belt of the strong" pictures the disarming of the powerful. They read the psalm and Job side by side without merging their settings, since each uses the words in its own way.

verses.text: He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death.
verses.arminianNotes: "He uncovers deep things out of darkness." Arminian readers see God's knowledge reaching into what is hidden, bringing out "to light the shadow of death." Nothing is concealed from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this power to uncover hidden things is part of why Job wants a hearing before God. If God sees everything, he can also see Job's innocence.

verses.text: He increases the nations, and he destroys them. He enlarges the nations, and he leads them captive.
verses.arminianNotes: "He increases the nations, and he destroys them." Arminian readers see God's rule over the rise and fall of whole peoples, not only of individuals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the balance of the line: God enlarges nations and also "leads them captive." History itself is in God's hand. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth, and causes them to wander in a wilderness where there is no way.
verses.arminianNotes: "He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth." Arminian readers see leaders left to wander "in a wilderness where there is no way" when God withdraws understanding from them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Psalm 107:40 also speaks of causing princes "to wander in a trackless waste." Both passages picture rulers lost when God removes their wisdom.

verses.text: They grope in the dark without light. He makes them stagger like a drunken man.
verses.arminianNotes: "They grope in the dark without light." Arminian readers see the end of human pride: leaders who trusted their own wisdom stagger "like a drunken man" when God humbles them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this closes Job's description of God's sovereign power. Job knows this power well. His question, pressed in chapter 13, is why it seems turned against him.
